content: Syphilis is a systemic disease caused by the spirochete Treponema pallidum. It can be transmitted either congenitally (from mother to child in utero) or acquired through sexual contact or blood transfusion. Acquired syphilis is further classified into early and late stages. Early syphilis includes primary, secondary, and early latent stages, while late syphilis encompasses late latent syphilis, gummatous syphilis, neurosyphilis, and cardiovascular syphilis. Primary syphilis is characterized by the presence of an ulcer or chancre at the site of infection or inoculation. Secondary syphilis presents with a skin rash, condylomata lata, mucocutaneous lesions, and generalized lymphadenopathy. Treatment for syphilis often involves a single dose of 4 million units of benzathine penicillin G administered intramuscularly. Due to the volume of the dose, it is typically divided into two injections at separate sites. For pregnant patients allergic to penicillin, an alternative regimen includes erythromycin 500 mg orally four times daily for 14 days. In 2012, there were an estimated 6 million new cases of syphilis among individuals aged 15–49 years worldwide, with 18 million prevalent cases. Despite global efforts to screen and treat pregnant women for syphilis, the burden of congenital syphilis remains high. In 2012, syphilis was responsible for approximately 350,000 adverse pregnancy outcomes globally, including 143,000 early fetal deaths or stillbirths, 62,000 neonatal deaths, 44,000 preterm or low birth weight deliveries, and 102,000 infected infants. Evidence suggests that a single dose of penicillin is more effective than a triple dose in achieving serological cure, although the certainty of this evidence is low. Mother-to-child transmission rates were higher with two doses of benzathine penicillin G compared to one dose, but this finding is also uncertain. Benzathine penicillin G and procaine penicillin are highly effective in preventing adverse outcomes and are preferred over other antibiotics such as azithromycin and erythromycin, which do not cross the placental barrier and therefore fail to treat the fetus. Procaine penicillin, which crosses both the placental and blood-brain barriers, is considered a second-line treatment for pregnant women. The cost of benzathine penicillin G varies depending on local labor costs for preparation, with an average price of $28–$72 per dose. Ceftriaxone, while effective, is more expensive and requires daily injections, making it less cost-effective compared to benzathine penicillin. Azithromycin and erythromycin are less effective in preventing mother-to-child transmission due to their inability to cross the placental barrier. Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy. The acceptability of treatment varies among patients and healthcare providers. While most patients (~80%) accept injections, weekly injections are preferred over daily ones. Some patients and healthcare workers express aversion to injections due to fear of allergic reactions. In practice, there is variability in the acceptability of treatment across different countries and settings. The feasibility of implementing syphilis treatment depends on the availability of benzathine penicillin G. Stock-outs of this medication should be avoided, as syphilis during pregnancy can lead to severe complications for the fetus or newborn. In cases where benzathine penicillin is unavailable, alternative treatments such as erythromycin, ceftriaxone, or azithromycin may be used with caution, but these require additional treatment for the newborn after delivery. The overall quality of evidence for syphilis treatment in pregnant women is very low, with limited studies and small sample sizes. Most studies do not specify the stage of syphilis (early or late) in pregnant women. Evidence from non-pregnant adults and adolescents has been used to inform recommendations for pregnant women. Penicillins remain the most effective treatment, as they cross the placental barrier and reduce the risk of mother-to-child transmission. The development of an oral therapy that can cross the placental and blood-brain barriers and requires a short course of treatment is a priority for future research. Trials investigating the appropriate dosages and effectiveness of ceftriaxone for early and late syphilis should also be conducted.
